evidence.claim: Route 244 is a rural northeastern Connecticut road linking Eastford with Pomfret.
evidence.quote: Route 244 is a secondary state highway in rural Northeastern Connecticut. It connects the towns of Eastford (at Route 198) and Pomfret (at Route 97).

evidence.claim: Known as the Boston Turnpike, it runs east, bends northeast and returns to an eastward course.
evidence.quote: Known as The Boston Turnpike, it turns northeast before falling back on an eastward track.

evidence.claim: The designated scenic section begins at Ragged Hill Road in Pomfret and ends at Route 97.
evidence.quote: The section of Route 244 from Ragged Hill Road in Pomfret to the eastern terminus is designated a scenic road.

evidence.claim: This road once belonged to the Middle Boston Post Road, one of the principal connections from Hartford to Boston and Providence.
evidence.quote: Route 244 was, at one time, part of the Middle Boston Post Road and was one of the principal roads connecting the city of Hartford in Connecticut to Boston in Massachusetts and Providence in Rhode Island.

evidence.claim: It became the privately operated Boston Turnpike toll road in 1797, then returned to public-road status in 1879.
evidence.quote: It was established as a private toll road known as the Boston Turnpike in 1797 and reverted to a public road in 1879.

evidence.claim: State responsibility came in 1962 as unsigned State Road 622; the posted Route 244 designation followed in 1988.
evidence.quote: On February 1, 1988, the road changed from unsigned State Road 622 (which became a state road in 1962) to Route 244.

evidence.claim: Follow the scenic section east from Ragged Hill Road toward Pomfret Center.
evidence.quote: The section of Route 244 from Ragged Hill Road in Pomfret to the eastern terminus is designated a scenic road.

evidence.claim: The final approach parallels Vineyard Valley Golf Club before meeting Route 97.
evidence.quote: Route 244 then intersects several minor roads before traveling parallel to the Vineyard Valley Golf Club as it intersects and ends at Route 97 in Pomfret Center.

evidence.claim: There, Route 244 ends, and northbound Route 97 continues toward US 44 and Route 169.
evidence.quote: Northbound Route 97 serves as the continuation of the road towards U.S. Route 44 and Route 169.

evidence.claim: Stone foundations remain where Bara-Hack’s houses and farms once stood, with forest covering most former fields and streets.
evidence.quote: The majority of the former fields and streets of Bara-Hack have been overgrown by forest. And only the stone foundations remain from the houses and farms.

evidence.claim: Johnathan Randall and Obediah Higinbotham settled here with their families in 1778 after fleeing British advances in Rhode Island.
evidence.quote: Bara-Hack was settled in 1778 by Johnathan Randall Esq. and Obediah Higinbotham, two colonists of English ancestry. They and their families fled the Randall homestead and farm, situated on the coast of Cranston, Rhode Island, after the British advances of the Battle of Rhode Island of 1778 deemed it too dangerous for them to stay.

evidence.claim: On land Randall had purchased in 1776, they established farms, a water-powered mill and a business making spinning wheels for textile production.
evidence.quote: They settled on land in Pomfret, Connecticut previously purchased by Randall in 1776, and there they built their homes, farms and livelihoods, including a water wheel-powered mill, a business which produced spinning wheels for the production of textiles

evidence.claim: The settlement was abandoned by 1890.
evidence.quote: The community was abandoned by 1890

evidence.claim: Its shared burial ground remains intact, but the site is private property.
evidence.quote: The cemetery is still intact.

evidence.claim: That connection has its own sequence of names: the Abington-to-Pomfret Center road became State Highway 345 in 1922, Route 201 in 1932 and part of Route 97 in 1934.
evidence.quote: In 1922, the road from Abington to Pomfret Center along modern Route 97 was designated as State Highway 345.

evidence.claim: Along Route 169, the Pomfret Street Historic District includes houses that became school buildings and cottages that outlasted their inn.
evidence.quote: The Pomfret Street Historic District is a historic district roughly along Pomfret Street (Route 169), from Bradley Road to Woodstock Road

evidence.claim: The Rectory School’s main building began as a house built in 1792 and once owned by Col. Thomas Grosvenor.
evidence.quote: Its main building is a converted house, built in 1792, once belonging to Col. Thomas Grosvenor

evidence.claim: Pomfret School occupies brick Georgian and Colonial Revival buildings designed by Ernest Flagg in the early twentieth century.
evidence.quote: It now includes brick Georgian and Colonial Revival buildings built during the first decade of the 20th century, designed by New York architect Ernest Flagg

evidence.claim: The Ben Grosvenor Inn was demolished in 1960, but Orchard Cottage and Olive Cottage remain as school dormitories.
evidence.quote: The Ben Grosvenor Inn grounds and outbuildings are in the district, but the Inn itself was demolished in 1960. Remaining buildings include Orchard Cottage and Olive Cottage, now used as dormitories by Pomfret School.

evidence.claim: The families also established a small burial ground for members of both households.
evidence.quote: and a small burial ground that would be shared by individual members of both families.

evidence.claim: Flagg also designed Clark Chapel, a Romanesque building from 1908, among the district’s school architecture.
evidence.quote: including the Romanesque 1908 Clark Chapel.
